priorities.movementBuildingText: We collaborate and network with other rights-based groups and networks to build a resilient intersex movement, enhancing the visibility of intersex persons over time
priorities.researchAdvocacyText: We conduct thorough research to understand the human rights issues affecting the communities we serve. We document human rights violations, collect data, and gather testimonies from affected individuals to build evidence for advocacy campaigns.
priorities.publicEngagementsText: We organize events to improve the perception of the public on variations of sex characteristics and overcome structural barriers towards reducing all forms of stigma & discrimination, and other human rights violations against intersex persons.
priorities.capacityBuildingText: We provide a comprehensive roadmap for systems strengthening aimed at organizational development,. By integrating best practices and emerging technology, we equip both intersex persons and our team with essential life competency skills.

priorities.srhrText: We develop and implement comprehensive sexuality education programs that provide accurate information about sexual and reproductive health, including topics such as contraception, HIV and STI prevention, consent, gender equality, and reproductive rights.

whatWeDo.raiseAwarenessText: Educate the public, policymakers, healthcare professionals, and communities about intersex variations and the harmful effects of genital manipulation surgeries. Raise awareness about the rights of intersex people and the importance of bodily autonomy and self-determination.
whatWeDo.trainingHealthcareText: Provide training and education for healthcare professionals on intersex variations, human rights principles, and best practices for supporting intersex patients and families. Advocate for culturally competent and affirming healthcare services for intersex individuals.
whatWeDo.advocacyLegalText: Advocate for legal protections against non-consensual medical interventions on intersex individuals, including genital surgeries. Work to ensure that laws and policies uphold the rights of intersex people to make informed decisions about their bodies and healthcare.
whatWeDo.psychosocialSupportText: We provide essential psychosocial support to individuals navigating life's challenges by offering a safe space where persons can share experiences, seek guidance, and find emotional comfort. Our programs prioritize mental well-being, resilience, and a sense of belonging, with the aim of empowering individuals to embrace their true selves.
whatWeDo.medicalEthicsText: Advocate for the development and implementation of medical ethics guidelines that prohibit non-consensual genital surgeries on intersex infants and children. Promote patient-centered care and informed decision-making in healthcare settings.
whatWeDo.empowermentText: We equip individuals with the tools, resources, and knowledge they need to strengthen themselves through life skills competency training, leadership training, and mentorship programs. Our goal is to ensure that every person pursues their dreams and makes a positive impact in their communities.

about.historyText:
Intersex Nigeria was established on November 25th, 2019, by Obioma Chukwuike, in response to the critical need for dedicated support, advocacy, and visibility for intersex persons in Nigeria. The organization was born out of a recognition of the systemic challenges and societal stigmas faced by the intersex community.

Since its inception, Intersex Nigeria has worked tirelessly to advocate for the rights of intersex persons, striving to create a society where they can enjoy bodily integrity and autonomy without fear of discrimination or stigma. By employing a feminist lens, we have engaged in community organizing, conducted research, and spearheaded public advocacy efforts, significantly advancing the rights and well-being of intersex persons in Nigeria.

We have made remarkable progress in raising public awareness and understanding of intersex issues. Through advocacy, social media campaigns, youth-focused sensitization, workshops, and community outreach programs, we have aimed to dispel myths and stereotypes surrounding people with variations in sex characteristics and promote a climate of acceptance and respect.
about.visionText: Our vision is to see a society where intersex persons, from birth, have rights to bodily integrity and autonomy and are free from stigma and discrimination.
about.missionText: To create an enabling society that promotes the visibility, inclusion, bodily autonomy, sexual and reproductive health including mental well-being and human rights of intersex persons in Nigeria, through community organizing, research, advocacy, and public engagements using a feminist lens.

objectives.awarenessText: To raise awareness about intersex issues and promote understanding of intersex variations through educational resources, and engagement.
objectives.advocacyText: To advocate for policies that protect the rights of intersex individuals, including the right to bodily integrity and autonomy.
objectives.communityText: To build a supportive community for intersex individuals in Nigeria, offering resources, peer support, and a platform for shared experiences.
objectives.healthcareText: To work towards improving healthcare outcomes for intersex individuals by advocating for informed, consensual, and culturally competent healthcare practices.
objectives.researchText: To conduct and support research on intersex issues in Nigeria, contributing to a body of knowledge that can inform policy, practice, and public understanding.

faq.intro: Find answers to some of the most common questions about intersex individuals, their rights, and how to support them. If you have more questions, feel free to reach out to us.
faq.q1: Is intersex the same thing as 'Trangender'?
faq.a1: Intersex relates to innate variations in biological sex characteristics, while transgender refers to a gender identity. Being a transgender person means to have an internal, deeply-held sense of being a man, woman, both, or neither. A transgender person has a gender identity that is different from the sex they were assigned at birth. For example, a person who was assigned female at birth (AFAB) but identifies as a man is a transgender man. It has nothing to do with their physical body, but rather with who they are on the inside.
faq.q2: Is intersex the same thing as “Hermaphrodite”?
faq.a2:
No. “Hermaphrodite” is not the same as intersex. The word came from mythology and should not be used to describe an intersex person.
Hermaphrodite means an organism that produces both male and female gametes, while intersex is an umbrella terms of persons born with innate variations in their sex characteristics (gonads, genitals, hormones, or chromosomal patterns) that do not fit into the typical binary definitions of male or female bodies.
Even though there are many intersex variations, a person can't have both a fully developed/functional penis and vagina.
faq.q3: Is intersex the same thing as “Disorder of Sex Development”?
faq.a3:
The term “Disorder of sex development” (DSD) is still common in medical settings. Many intersex people and and human rights advocates reject the term “DSD” because it supports the idea that intersex bodies are wrong and up to doctors to “fix the unnatural”
The word 'disorder' frames a natural biological variation as a medical problem or a pathology. It implies that something is broken and needs to be 'fixed', which is apathologizing approach. Intersex bodies are not 'wrong' or 'unnatural'; they are an integral part of human diversity, just like variations in height, eye color, or hair type. By labeling this as a disorder, the medical community gives itself a reason to intervene, even when there's no health risk.
faq.a4:
People born with innate variations in sex development have healthy sex variations that are biological. Also, there hasn’t been any proven studies that show intersex as a defect.
The word 'defect' implies a flaw, an error, or something that is not functioning properly. Labeling an intersex trait as a 'defect' wrongly suggests that the person is broken or incomplete and their body is somehow 'wrong'.
All intersex people are perfectly healthy. While some variations may come with specific medical considerations, the variations themselves are not inherently a sickness or a flaw. The problem often lies not with the body, but with societal expectations and medical practices that treat these healthy variations as something that needs to be 'fixed' and fit into a rigid sex binary.
faq.a5:
Intersex is a natural biological variations in sex characteristics, and it is not a medical emergency.
While intersex conditions are often surrounded by misconceptions and stigma, it’s essential to recognize that being intersex is a normal aspect of every human diversity. Medical emergencies can arise in anyone, regardless of their sex characteristics or gender identity. For instance, an individual may experience health issues such as infections, chronic diseases, injuries, or genetic disorders, which can affect anyone, and that still has not reduced them being a human. The key is to provide appropriate healthcare that respects the individual’s identity and needs.
faq.a6:
Do intersex babies, teenagers, and adults need surgery?
No, most intersex people don't ever in any way need surgery as a solution. Even While some intersex variations may require surgery for urgent medical reasons, most do not. The issue lies in the practice of performing medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants and adolescents as it violates their bodily autonomy, and these surgeries are performed to make a an intersex person's body conform to a typical male or female appearance.
faq.q7: What are the physical and psychological effects of non-consensual surgeries on intersex infants and children?
faq.a7:
Non-consensual surgeries performed on intersex infants and children lead to significant physical complications, including scarring, loss of sensation, urinary incontinence, sexual dysfunction, and the risk of additional surgeries later in life.
Psychologically, these individuals may experience trauma, shame, depression, and anxiety, which can hinder their ability to form a positive sense of self and body image. It is crucial to prioritize informed consent and the well-being of intersex individuals, allowing them to make decisions about their own bodies as they grow and develop.
faq.q8: Is intersex a taboo or a bad omen?
faq.a8:
Intersex is a biological and innate human diversity in sex characteristics, and it is not a taboo.
The misconception that being intersex is a taboo or a bad omen is a result of societal and cultural un-understanding. For centuries, societies have operated on a strict binary of male and female. Anything that falls outside this norm is often misunderstood, feared, stigmatized, and seen out of the ordinary; due to these views, they see an intersex person as a sign of a curse, a punishment from a deity, or a bad luck charm.
faq.q9: How do I know if I am Intersex?
faq.a9:
A person can be intersex without knowing it. Here are the most common ways for a person to notice that their body is different:
● At birth, due to their physical genital differences;
● At puberty, when changes began to happen in the body, it happen too early, in unexpected ways, or not at all;
● In adulthood, when infertility or other changes began to reveal internal differences and
● Learnings about adults' medical records covered up
● During medical check ups.
Also, there are people who do have differences in their sex traits and have never heard the word intersex or any knowledge about who they are.
faq.q10: Can Intersex people have children or get pregnant?
faq.a10:
Yes/maybe. Like any person, it depends on body parts. (And sometimes, help from technology.)
Creating an embryo requires a sperm from a testis and an egg from an ovary. The developing fetus then needs a place to grow, which is usually a uterus. Advancements in medical technology have created diverse pathways for that to happen even for non-intersex persons. However, it is not possible for any human to reproduce on their own; it always involves at least one other person to make it happen. Intersex persons can also have children through pregnancy, adoption,etc.
faq.q11: Message to a parent of guardian of an Intersex person
faq.a11:
A child needs emotional, care, and psychological support. It's important to create an open and honest conversation about the bodily differences with your child and within the family. Hiding the truth teaches a child that their body is something to be ashamed of.
Family should seek informed information from intersex advocates, adults, and organizations as these spaces and conversation can offer invaluable guidance and a sense of belonging for both you and your child.
Like any child, an intersex child can be raised socially as any child without the need for unnecessary surgery. Decisions regarding non-life-saving surgical interventions should be delayed/postponed until the person is old enough to understand and allow for informed consent. This approach honors your child's autonomy and their right to make decisions about their own body.

whatIsIntersex.subtitle: Learning about the natural diversity of human sex characteristics and promoting awareness. Let us Understand Intersex.
whatIsIntersex.definitionP1: Intersex is an umbrella term for the spectrum of innate variations of sex characteristics that naturally occur within the human species. Intersex people are born with variations of sex characteristics (such as genitals, gonads, reproductive organs, hormonal and chromosomal patterns) that are more diverse than stereotypical definitions of male or female bodies.
whatIsIntersex.definitionP2: Some intersex traits are noticed at birth, while others may not be discovered until puberty, later in life, or never known.
whatIsIntersex.genderDesc: Gender is a concept that refers to socially constructed roles, behaviors, expressions, and identities that a given society considers appropriate for individuals based on their perceived or assigned sex at birth.
whatIsIntersex.sexCharacteristicsDesc: Sex characteristics are physical features relating to sex. Everyone is born with innate primary and secondary sex characteristics.
whatIsIntersex.primaryDesc: present at birth and includes genitals, gonads (internal reproductive organs), chromosomes and hormones.
whatIsIntersex.secondaryDesc: develops during puberty e.g facial hair, breast, voice pitch, muscle development,etc.
whatIsIntersex.sexDefinition: Sex is the biological categorization of a person based on their sex characteristics.
whatIsIntersex.statsDescP1: Intersex variations are a natural and healthy part of human biodiversity, not a rare anomaly. Experts says that 1.7 percent of the world's population are intersex, highlighting that intersex traits occur in about 1 in 60 births worldwide, making them as common as people with left handedness.
whatIsIntersex.statsDescP2: This challenges the notion that intersex is an exceptional difference and underscores its status as a natural human variation.
whatIsIntersex.variationsDesc: Intersex variations can be present in various ways, visible at birth, during puberty, or later in life. Some intersex persons live through life or even die without knowing that they are intersex. Some of the common intersex variations include:

variations.aisDesc: These are variations in people with XY chromosomes who are resistant to male hormones and develop typically female or mixed characteristics.
variations.cahDesc: This a genetic variation that can typically affect hormone production, leading to variations in secondary sex characteristics, like excess hair etc. There several levels of CAH that currently exist.
variations.ovotestesDesc: This variation indicates the presence of both ovarian and testicular tissues in the same persons.
variations.klinefelterDesc: A variation where individuals assigned male at birth have an extra X chromosome.
variations.turnerDesc: A variation where persons who are assigned female at birth who lack a second sex chromosome.
variations.fiveAlphaDesc: This is a variation where people assigned male at birth have atypical genital (ambiguous genitalia) development due to reduced hormone conversion. this variation often has normal ovarian tissue with atrophic testicular tissue
variations.hypospadiasDesc: This is a variation where an individuals opening of the urethra is not at the tip of the penis, but it is on the underside of the penis and is sometimes located further back near the scrotum.
variations.swyerDesc: This is a variation where persons born with XY chromosomes, but their gonads have not developed into testes. Since they do not produce testosterone, their body develops a vulva and vagina and they often develop a uterus and fallopian tubes as well. People with Swyer Syndrome do menstruate (without ovulating) if they receive estrogen therapy.

intersectionality.aboutHeading: At The Intersection – An Intersex Nigeria E-Resource Hub
intersectionality.aboutP1: At the intersection is a learning hub and subsidiary of Intersex Nigeria. We are dedicated to promoting and advocating for the sexual reproductive health, self-determination, bodily autonomy, and overall human rights of intersex people in Nigeria.
intersectionality.aboutP2: Through community building, advocacy, evidence-based research, empowerment, educational and informational resources on intersex-related issues, we engage with the public, partners, stakeholders, and our community.
intersectionality.aboutP3: Our goal is to create a society where intersex bodies are not stigmatised and discriminated, and where intersex rights are recognised and respected.
intersectionality.whatIsP1: Intersectionality conceptualizes the ways that individuals and groups face multiple forms of discrimination or privilege at once based on the disadvantages (intersectionally marginalized) or advantages (intersectionally privileged) associated with their identities within two or more social categories (such as sex, sexual orientation, ethnicity, tribe, descent or inherited status, age, class, disability or health status), rather than a single category. Intersectionality exposes the socio-structural nature of discrimination and inequality and the role of exclusionary social and cultural norms in including or marginalizing certain categories (Sosa, 2017, p. 16).
intersectionality.whatIsP2: Individuals belong to more than one social category, and as a result, they can simultaneously experience both discrimination and privilege. Different combinations of these social categories may increase or decrease the likelihood that a person will experience systemic oppression and discrimination.
intersectionality.whatIsP3: As a framework or lens, intersectionality is used to analyze social complexity and address the intersection of social categories at the individual level and the overlapping and interlocking systems of power (laws, policies, state governments, political unions, religious institutions, and media) and oppression that impact different groups in distinct ways at structural levels (Bowleg, 2012). As a tool, intersectionality is used to engineer appropriate interventions to address marginalization and social exclusion.
intersectionality.why1Text: Intersectionality allows us to understand that individuals are shaped by multiple, overlapping social identities, such as gender, ethnicity, tribe, sexual orientation, class, and disability. For intersex and persons with diverse identities, these identities often intersect in ways that compound their experiences of discrimination and marginalization. By adopting an intersectional approach, we can better recognize and address the unique challenges faced by each individual within the intersex community.
intersectionality.why2Text: Many systems of oppression-such as sexism, tribalism, homophobia, transphobia, and ableism-are interconnected and cannot be fully understood or dismantled in isolation. Intersectionality helps us to see how these systems operate together to create complex layers of disadvantage. This awareness empowers us to tackle the root causes of inequality more effectively, ensuring that no one is left behind in our advocacy efforts.
intersectionality.why3Text: Intersectionality fosters inclusivity by valuing and respecting the full spectrum of human diversity. It encourages us to create spaces where all voices are heard, all experiences are validated, and all individuals are supported in their journey toward self-empowerment. This approach aligns with our commitment to building a supportive and united community for intersex persons with diverse identities and multiple experiences in Nigeria.
intersectionality.why4Text: By embracing intersectionality, we amplify the voices of those who are often the most marginalized. This includes individuals who might experience multiple forms of discrimination due to their intersecting identities. Our work aims to elevate these voices, ensuring that they are not only heard but also actively involved in shaping the solutions to the issues that impact their lives.

0.title: Official Statement: Intersex Nigeria Responds to the New International Olympic Committee (IOC) Policy on Sex Testing; Harm and Discrimination on Intersex Women
0.subtitle: Policy on the Protection of the Female (Women’s) Category in Olympic Sport
0.description: Intersex Nigeria stands in opposition to the IOC policy released on 26 March 2026, which mandates one-time SRY genetic sex testing and undermines the privacy, dignity, and rights of women athletes.
intro: Intersex Nigeria stands in opposition to the International Olympic Committee (IOC) policy released on 26 March, 2026 which discriminates against transgender and intersex women with Olympic dreams through a mandated one-time SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) genetic sex testing that invades the privacy and dignity of all women athletes. While framed as a measure for "fairness," this policy represents a direct attack on the privacy, dignity, and human rights of intersex women athletes across the globe.

Intersex is an umbrella term used to describe people who are born with innate sex characteristics such as chromosomes, hormones, gonads, or genitals that do not fit typical binary definitions of male or female bodies. They make up to approximately 1.7% of the world population. We assert that sex characteristics exist on diverse spectrum and can’t be reduced to binary experiences.

concerns.title: Unscientific Foundations
concerns.body: Experts, including the scientist who discovered the SRY gene, stated the SRY gene is not a definitive indicator of biological sex or athletic advantage. They noted that its presence does not determine how a body functions or responds to testosterone.

concerns.title: Violations of Privacy and Dignity
concerns.body: Requiring a one-time genetic testing to participate in sports violates the fundamental privacy of women and girls, exposing them to invasive medical scrutiny and the risk of being forcibly outed regarding their intersex status, or they may not even be aware of their own intersex variation, leading to extreme public scrutiny and humiliation.

concerns.title: Coerced Medical Intervention
concerns.body: Similar past policies have forced athletes to undergo invasive physical exams or alter their natural hormone levels through medication, often leading to declining health and psychological trauma.

concerns.title: Discriminatory Exclusion
concerns.body: While the policy offers rare exceptions for specific variations, it effectively denies many intersex women with XY chromosomes or higher testosterone levels participation in Olympic sport.

concerns.title: Safeguarding Risks for Youth
concerns.body: As many elite athletes begin their careers as children, this policy creates a safeguarding risk by requiring the investigation of children's bodies and the disclosure of intimate health information, which can lead to permanent harm to their dignity and mental health.

0.conclusion: Intersex Nigeria calls on sports governing bodies to recognize that intersex women are women. All athletes deserve the right to play the sports they love free from discrimination, invasive testing, and medical policing.

why-menstrual-healthcare-for-intersex-pe.title: Why Menstrual Healthcare for Intersex People Matters
why-menstrual-healthcare-for-intersex-pe.text: When we talk about menstrual health, many people only think of female persons. But not everyone who menstruates is a female person. Some intersex people also menstruate. Their needs are often ignored in health programmes and public conversations.
why-menstrual-healthcare-for-intersex-pe.post:
When we talk about menstrual health, many people only think of female persons. But not everyone who menstruates is a female person. Some intersex people also menstruate. Their needs are often ignored in health programmes and public conversations. Even schools, which should be institutions of learning, rarely include intersex persons in their curriculum.
Intersex people are born with bodies that do not fit the typical definitions of male or female. This can include genitalia, but also chromosomes and hormones. Some intersex people have a uterus and experience periods. Others do not. But for those who do, it is important that they have access to correct information, support and safe products.
For intersex people who menstruate, many of them face shame, confusion or silence when their periods start. For intersex people who menstruate, the onset of periods is often accompanied by shame, confusion and silence. This is not just from a lack of information, but from systemic erasure. In many communities, menstruation is framed strictly as a "female issue," leaving no room for the experiences of intersex people whose bodies may not conform to binary expectations. As a result, in the situation where an intersex person begin menstruating, they are often met with disbelief, ridicule or outright denial of their bodily autonomy. Some are pressured to hide their experiences to protect their families from perceived social shame, while others are told that their bodies are “wrong” or in need of medical correction. These cause fear, stress and mental health issues.
Some Intersex men who experience symptoms linked to menstruation, such as cramping, spotting or bleeding may feel a deep discomfort with their body. This is called dysphoria. It is the feeling that your body is not matching who you know yourself to be. It can be painful, especially when health workers dismiss their symptoms and/or belittle them. They are left feeling alone and confused.
Most health workers are not trained to care for intersex people. Some do not even know what intersex means. In our report on ]**Medical Practices and Experiences Surrounding Intersex Births in Nigerian Hospitals**] we found that 74% of healthcare professionals indicated that their hospitals had no specific approach to managing intersex cases.
This leads to misinformed treatment or harmful advice. For example, telling someone to take hormonal medicine to stop their bleeding without checking their full health background to understand the root cause or even asking the person if they even want that. Another is by using language that makes them feel ashamed, such as calling them a mystery insisting on them being "fixed".
Menstrual health education must include intersex people. Just as teaching boys about menstruation helps reduce stigma, incorporating the experiences of intersex individuals creates greater understanding and inclusivity. In Kenya, initiatives like Jinsiangu’s [**InclusiFit**[ are leading the way by addressing menstrual hygiene needs specific to intersex persons.
Safe toilets, pain relief and access to pads are not gender issues. They are health needs. Intersex people must be included in menstrual health programmes. For example, a school toilet should be safe for both a boy who menstruates and a girl who menstruates. This can be done by making restrooms gender neutral or by making disposal bins available in all toilet stalls to make disposal of sanitary items easy. It should not be based on gender, but on need.
Also, language matters. Saying “women and girls” all the time can leave others out. A better term is “people who menstruate.” This helps include everyone without confusion.
If we say menstrual health is for all, then we must mean it. Intersex people are part of that “all.” Their needs are not extra. They are basic. This world menstrual health hygiene day and beyond, we must all work towards including intersex persons in menstrual healthcare.

the-intersection-of-our-narratives-in-th.title: The Intersection of Our Narratives in The Face of Discrimination
the-intersection-of-our-narratives-in-th.text: Discrimination against women and girls is a pervasive issue that undermines human rights and socio-economic development worldwide. Despite significant progress in gender equality, millions continue to face systemic barriers, including gender-based violence, economic inequality, social exclusion and patriarchy.
the-intersection-of-our-narratives-in-th.post:
“*Nothing for us without us. Nothing for women without the involvement and inclusion*”. Joyce Banda.
Discrimination against women and girls is a pervasive issue that undermines human rights and socio-economic development worldwide. Despite significant progress in gender equality, millions continue to face systemic barriers, including gender-based violence, economic inequality, social exclusion and patriarchy. The “Orange the World” campaign highlights the urgency of addressing these injustices, raising awareness and advocating for change. 
Discrimination against women/girls is manifested in various forms, such as: 
**Gender-Based Violence:** According to the Nigerian Demographic and Health Survey, 31% of women/girls aged 15-49 experienced physical violence, and UNICEF Nigeria 1 in 4 girls experienced sexual violence before the age of 18 in her lifetime, often at the hands of intimate partners. This violence not only causes physical harm but also leads to long-term psychological trauma and distortion in life. 
**Economic Disparities:** They are represented in low-paying or unemployable jobs and are less likely to hold leadership positions. The gender pay gap remains a significant barrier to financial independence. 
**Social Exclusion:** Cultural norms and stereotypes often dictate their roles, limiting their access to education, healthcare, and participation in public life. This exclusion perpetuates cycles of poverty and dependence. 
Growing up in the northern part of Nigeria I have seen and witnessed families consisting of young women/girls and men/boys but these women/girls had aspirations and, dreams of influence, changed. Then they are forced into early marriage and childbirth, divorced, and unrepairable medical health conditions, with the belief that her primary role should be as a wife and a mother. The familial pressure to conform her to her role left her feeling isolated and unworthy of her ambitions.
These stories reflect a broader pattern of discrimination that hinders them from their basic human rights. Their narratives of survival and resilience are crucial as they inspire us to challenge the status quo and advocate for rights. 
The consequences of violence against her extend beyond them, affecting families and communities. These women/girls often face stigma, isolation, fear, and a lack of support, which can hinder their ability to seek help and perpetuate the continuous cycle of violence against them often transcending generations. Moreover, the discrimination they face has broader societal implications, including decreased economic productivity, increased cost of living, and perpetuation of gender inequality.
Addressing the prevalence of discrimination and violence requires comprehensive awareness and strategic campaigns. These initiatives should focus on educating communities about the signs of abuse, available resources, and the importance of supporting her. Engaging men/boys in these conversations is crucial for fostering a culture of respect, accountability, and responsibility. 
To combat discrimination and violence, we must examine existing policies and practices. Nigeria has made strides in developing legal frameworks to protect her rights under the Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act, yet enforcement and Implementation remain a significant challenge. Advocacy efforts must focus on holding the Government accountable for enforcing these laws and ensuring that resources are allocated to support them. Additionally, community-based programs that educate persons about their rights and provide access to legal assistance can empower them to stand up against discrimination. 
Community engagement plays a vital role in combating discrimination. Grassroots initiatives can foster solidarity and empower her by creating safe spaces for dialogue and support. 
Workshops and Training, Collective Campaigns and Intersectional advocacy is vital in addressing discrimination, as it recognizes that persons experience discrimination in multifaceted ways. Factors such as sex, race, class, and sexual orientation, intersect to create unique challenges for different groups of women/girls, gender minorities and intersex persons. This approach acknowledges that the experiences of a married/single woman/girl, or an intersex person cannot be fully understood by examining only one aspect of their identity in isolation. We embracing an intersectional framework, can ensure that our advocacy efforts are inclusive, reflecting the diverse realities and needs of all persons that are discriminated. This inclusivity not only enhances our understanding of the systemic and intersectional barriers that different communities face but also strengthens our collective efforts to promote equity and justice for everyone. 
The fight against discrimination and violence toward her is far from over. The “Orange the World” (16 Days of Activism) campaign reminds us of our collective responsibility in creating a safer, more equitable society. By sharing our stories, advocating for policy changes, and engaging in community action, we can pave the way for a future free from violence and discrimination. 
As individuals and communities, we must commit to raising our voices and taking action. Whether through our voices, activism, or support for local initiatives, every effort contributes to the larger movement for gender equality. Let us stand together in solidarity and work towards a world where all women and girls can thrive without fear of discrimination or violence.

unite-to-end-violence-against-women-and-.title: UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls
unite-to-end-violence-against-women-and-.text: Violence against women and girls is one of the world’s oldest evil. The United Nations estimates that 1 in 3 women experience one form of violence or the other in their lifetime; this is estimated 736 million women worldwide, making violence against women and girls a global pandemic.
unite-to-end-violence-against-women-and-.post:
Violence against women and girls is one of the world’s oldest evil. The United Nations estimates that 1 in 3 women experience one form of violence or the other in their lifetime; this is estimated 736 million women worldwide, making violence against women and girls a global pandemic. World Bank highlights that 35% of women globally have experienced either physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence or non-partner sexual violence. Additionally ]**World Health Organisation**] estimated that over 200 million women globally have experienced female genital mutilation without a specific statistics for intersex persons. 
The fight for a just and equal society where women and girls as well as intersex persons thrive have been consistent through the years. However, the strong force of stigma, which is pervasive but yet under-recognised still finds subtle ways to influence this fight. Stigma fuels misconceptions, perpetuates harmful stereotypes directed at survivors of violence, particularly women, girls and intersex persons and ultimately serves as a barrier to achieving true equality and safety for all.  Stigma often lead to a culture of silence, shame, and fear, preventing many survivors of violence, especially women, girls and intersex people from seeking help, accessing critical support, and having bodily autonomy. 
The culture of [**silence**[ surrounding gender-based violence (GBV) is perhaps the most immediate and damaging consequence of stigma. Survivors are often unable to speak owing to fear of being judged, punished or excluded from social settings. In Nigeria and many other countries in the world, }**patriarchal system**} holds supreme and the structure of patriarchy promotes a shame-based silence that prevents or discourages women form speaking out. Also, in many cultures, survivors of violence are told to suck it up, warned against seeking help and often threatened with further violence like ostracism, physical abuse, “corrective” rape, etc. They are told that speaking up will bring shame to the family and are blamed for the violence they experience. This causes a continuous cycle of abuse as survivors tend to remain silent to avoid bringing stigma onto themselves or their loved ones, even when they desperately need help. Social exclusion in the face of violence as a survivor can not be overemphasised. Survivors often lose support systems, are stigmatised in social structures like work places, schools and places of worship; leaving them more vulnerable. This, again, leads survivors to a hole of silence, remaining in the place of abuses. 
Shame and fear are some of the most damaging consequences of stigma. Women and girls are often made to feel responsible for the abuse they face through societal expectation of dresses, who to love, actions and behaviour which further promote a system that celebrates abusers and stigmatise survivors and consequently, silences survivors from reaching out for the help and legal support they deserve. In the light of these, the need to deconstruct the elements that fuel stigma in the face of gender-based violence is imperative. 
A critical first step is to create a safe space where survivors can share their experience without the feeling of shame, fear or thought of being judged. By our actions, words and behaviours we can help survivors of abuse feel that they will be believed, supported, and protected, not blamed, dismissed or subjected to more violence. 
Secondly, the culture of victim blaming must be challenged while holding perpetrators accountable. It is essential to amplify that violence on women, girls and intersex persons or anyone else is never the victim’s fault and women must be supported and shown that they are worthy of respect, dignity and justice. 
In conclusion, as we embark on this journey to **UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls**, it is imperative that we confront and dismantle the stigmas that threaten to undermine our progress. Together, let us challenge harmful societal norms, empower survivors, and ensure accountability of perpetrators. Only then can we create a world where all women, girls and intersex persons can live free from violence and discrimination, with dignity and respect for their rights.

gender-based-violence-against-intersex-p.title: Gender-Based Violence Against Intersex People: Hidden Realities and the Urgent Call for Justice
gender-based-violence-against-intersex-p.text: In the fight against gender-based violence, the experiences of intersex people are often overlooked, hidden in the shadows of the binary gender world. Intersex people, born with variations in sex characteristics that don’t fit typical male or female norms, face a unique set  of injustices that go largely unaddressed.
gender-based-violence-against-intersex-p.post:
In the fight against gender-based violence, the experiences of intersex people are often overlooked, hidden in the shadows of the binary gender world. Intersex people, born with variations in sex characteristics that don’t fit typical male or female norms, face a unique set  of injustices that go largely unaddressed. During this year’s 16 Days of Activism, it’s time to bring their stories to light and demand protection, dignity, and respect for intersex individuals everywhere. 
Despite feminist strides, ours is still not a society that supports and rewards individuals who do not conform to gender norms. Little boys are still kept in line with phrases like, “Don’t be a sissy.” Little girls and particularly older girls face fierce disapproval if they behave or dress too “boyishly.” This early punishment for simply expressing gender identity leaves many scars, but the experiences that lead  intersexual domestic violence survivors to believe that it’s normal for “people like me” to live with abuse only increase in magnitude as the intersex survivor matures. 
**The Invisible Violence of “Correction”** 
For many intersex persons, gender-based violence begins at birth. Doctors, often with the backing of family members, perform non-consensual “normalizing” surgeries on infants and young children. These surgeries aim to make a child’s body conform to societal expectations of male or female. The procedures may involve removing or altering genital tissue, reshaping organs, or administering hormones to “correct the body” irreversibly. 
The paper titled Trans and Intersex Survivors of Domestic Violence: Defining Terms, Barriers, & Responsibilities By Diana Courvant and Loree Cook-Daniels talks about a doctor who at an annual convention of the Society for the Scientific Study of Sexuality related the case of a girl child with a large clitoris sexually mutilated by her father, who was angered at the phallic proportions of his infant daughter’s clitoris. Amazingly, this doctor completed the child’s mutilation by performing a clitoridectomy and was using her story to justify surgery on infants in similar situations, rather than healing the child and calling attention to her abuse. Although these stories’ power is anecdotal and not statistical, they and others like them are widely known and retold among intersex individuals. Because of the extreme cruelty and casual indifference of authorities and institutions exemplified in these common stories, an intersex survivor may fear an unknown service institution more than a familiar abuser. 
**A Life in the Shadows: The Psychological Toll of Secrecy and Stigma** 
The psychological violence against intersex persons doesn’t end with childhood surgeries. From a young age, many are shamed, silenced, or pressured to keep their identities a secret. Imagine growing up in a world that insists you’re “different” in ways that make people uncomfortable. Families, often unprepared to understand or advocate for intersex rights, can unintentionally fuel this isolation. 
One U.S.- based intersex advocate described feeling “invisible” for years. “My parents tried to hide it from me,” they explained, “and so I felt like there was something wrong with me. It took years of unlearning and self-love to realize that I wasn’t broken.” The shame imposed by society often leads to mental health issues like depression, anxiety, and in extreme cases, suicidal ideation. 
**Intersex People at the Margins of Rights** 
Institutional discrimination compounds the trauma, as many countries including Nigeria don’t legally recognize intersex identities or protect intersex rights. Denied recognition and often forced to choose a binary gender, intersex individuals encounter obstacles in healthcare, legal systems, and workplaces. In Kenya, until 2020, intersex people couldn’t obtain identification that accurately reflected their identity, preventing access to basic services like education and healthcare. This legal erasure is yet another form of violence, keeping intersex people trapped in systems that deny their existence and rights. 
**The Road to Dignity: What Needs to Change** 
To end this cycle of gender based violence, we must confront the medical, social, and legal systems that violate the rights of intersex persons. Here’s how we can begin to create a safer world for intersex persons: 
1.	**End Non-Consensual Surgeries:** All children, including intersex children, have a right to bodily autonomy. We must urge medical systems to halt unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants and ensure that any medical interventions are based on consent and necessity, not outdated ideals of “normal.” 
2.	**Raise Awareness and Erase Stigma:** The shame and isolation imposed on intersex persons by society need to end. Through education, communities can learn that intersex characteristics are natural, diverse variations of human biology. Awareness campaigns can help shift the narrative from secrecy to acceptance. 
3.	**Advocate for Legal Protections and Recognition:** Governments must create laws that prohibit discrimination against intersex individuals and recognize intersex identities. Legal protections and rights are crucial to ensure that intersex people can live without fear of exclusion, discrimination, or violence. 
4.	**Center Intersex Voices:** Change will only be meaningful if intersex individuals are included in conversations about their own rights and welfare. From activism to policy making, intersex voices should lead the way in creating a society that celebrates, rather than hides, their identities.
**A Call to Action** 
As we participate in the 16 Days of Activism, let us not forget intersex people, whose stories are often silenced. Their fight for dignity, autonomy, and justice is as vital as any in the movement against gender-based violence. Stand with intersex persons. Share their stories. Demand an end to practices that violate their rights. Together, we can create a world where no one is forced to hide, and everyone’s identity is respected and protected. 
It’s time to shine a light on these hidden realities and make room for all identities in the global call for equality and justice.

towards-beijing-30-confronting-gender-ba.title: Towards Beijing +30: Confronting Gender-Based Violence Against Women and Girls in Their Diversity
towards-beijing-30-confronting-gender-ba.text: As the world enters the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence (GBV), this year’s theme, “Towards Beijing +30: UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls,” calls us to action with renewed urgency.
towards-beijing-30-confronting-gender-ba.post:
*When one woman is harmed, every woman—and the entire community—feels it.* 
As the world enters the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence (GBV), this year’s theme, “Towards Beijing +30: UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls,” calls us to action with renewed urgency. For marginalized women and girls—those who are poor, uneducated, queer, intersex, disabled, or facing language barriers—the fight against violence is not only about physical harm. It’s about dismantling systems of exclusion and discrimination that threaten both their physical safety and mental health. Over three decades since the Beijing Declaration, we must ask: What has truly changed? Has the system become a tool of oppression? Are we going to pretend it hasn’t? 
**The Mental Toll of GBV and Exclusion** 
 Across Nigeria and many African societies, GBV does more than harm bodies; it shatters minds and lives. Marginalized women and girls endure not only overt forms of violence but also the psychological damage caused by systemic discrimination and exclusion. When a young woman with a disability is denied access to school because she is seen as “too much work,” a queer woman faces harassment at work for not fitting into what the system demands, or an intersex person is shunned by their family for not fitting neatly into “male” or “female” categories, the toll on mental health is as real as any physical injury. These experiences deepen anxiety, depression, and a profound sense of isolation that can take years—if not a lifetime—to heal. 
 As I pen these words, I let my tears flow because every line reflects my own life and the lives of a community with similar, if not worse, experiences of true and intentional exclusion due to our differences. I know how poverty is used as a tool of oppression, how mental health struggles are dismissed as abstract and unreal. I see how we constantly live in fear of simply being because of a system designed to erase our identities, experiences, and realities. Yet, with these words, we continue to exist and claim our spaces through ink and action. 
 **Spotlighting African Women and Girls in Their Diversity** 
 For African women and girls in all their diversity, the impact of Gender Based Violence (GBV) is amplified by intersecting barriers. Those without financial resources, formal education, or community support are less likely to access mental health services and more likely to be silenced by societal stigma. In these conditions, ***GBV becomes both a cause and a consequence of broader social inequities, reinforcing a cycle of poverty, vulnerability, and mental health deterioration***. 
**Community Care as a Lifeline** 
 As we mark nearly 30 years since the historic Beijing Platform for Action, the call to address GBV through community-centered support has never been more critical. In Africa, community has always been a source of strength and healing. This tradition of collective care offers a foundation for innovative solutions that can uplift women and girls in their diversity, especially when access to formal services is limited. 
 Community care initiatives that address both GBV and mental health are essential. Women’s shelters, peer counseling networks, and safe spaces for queer and intersex youth can offer vital support, providing a safe haven from violence and a place to heal. These networks not only combat the effects of GBV but also work proactively to prevent violence through education, solidarity, and advocacy. In Nigeria, organizations supporting women from marginalized backgrounds have become powerful advocates, providing emotional support and championing policy changes that challenge violence in all its forms. There are feminists’ groups where resources are shared for wellbeing and care. As much as the feminist movements is shaping how women organizations ae becoming inclusive of the diverse women and girls, there so much work that needs to be done in combating the attitudes towards women and girls existing outside the binary. To My feminists’ sisters, we can do better. 
** Solutions from a Community Perspective** 
***While community care offers immediate relief, broader structural changes are needed to ensure that no woman or girl is left vulnerable to GBV.*** As the global CSOs speak on Cross Movement Solidarity for true inclusion, governments, policymakers, and civil society must work together to provide inclusive mental health resources and combat discriminatory practices in healthcare, education, and employment. For marginalized groups, this means that mental health support should be readily available in all local languages, disability-accessible, and culturally sensitive to different sexual orientations, sex characteristics and gender identities. 
 Community initiatives can only thrive when supported by inclusive laws and policies. For women and girls in their diversity, structural support must go beyond GBV laws and extend to socioeconomic opportunities, language access, and disability rights. Education campaigns targeting schools, workplaces, and communities can shift harmful mindsets, showing that mental health support is a right, not a privilege, and that every woman and girl deserves a life **free from violence and exclusion**. 
*Mental health care should never be a luxury!* 
**Calling for Collective Responsibility** 
This year’s 16 Days of Activism is a reminder that ending GBV requires collective action. Each of us has a role to play in creating a world where marginalized women and girls feel safe, supported, and empowered. We can educate ourselves and others about the challenges they face, support local organizations doing critical work, and speak out against all forms of exclusion and violence. When we unite in solidarity, we not only uplift individual women and girls but strengthen the very thread that holds our societies. 
 As we move toward Beijing +30, let us commit to a vision where no woman or girl in Nigeria or anywhere else in the world, is left to suffer in silence. By embracing community care and advocating for inclusive policies, we can build a future that honors the dignity, resilience, and mental well-being of all women and girls in their diversity. 
*We cannot continue to turn a blind eye to the double and triple jeopardy that women and girls in their diversity are faced with. We must be intentional about true inclusion in the fight to end GBV. Turning a blind eye to the fact that GBV is also enabled because women and girls are existing outside the binary, is inhumane and oppressive. Leaders at the helms of affairs must ensure not to overlook the double issue that confronts people like me, who do not look like a typical woman, and as a result, face multiple forms of violation and exclusion, impacting our emotional and mental well-being. You cannot continue to be on the fence or be diplomatic with issues of queer, intersex women, including women with visible and invisible disabilities. You cannot afford to be DIPLOMATIC!* 
 *In the end, healing from systemic exclusion and discrimination requires an intentional, United, compassionate approach and it is important to state that this is not just a call to end violence but a demand for true inclusion in the fight against GBV.* 
For real change, African governments, civil society, and health systems must recognize the link between discrimination, mental health, and gender-based violence, especially for marginalized women and girls. Policies must address underlying societal structures that perpetuate exclusion, with support for inclusive mental health services that cater to diverse identities and abilities. 
 TAKE ACTION, NOW!

photo-story-of-intersex-persons-in-niger.title: Photo Story of Intersex Persons in Nigeria
photo-story-of-intersex-persons-in-niger.text: Intersex-Nigeria was founded in November 2019 by Obioma Chukwuike to create public awareness and understanding of intersex people and to encourage community building among intersex persons. The advocacy is centered on the rights to bodily integrity, ending stigma and discrimination, creating visibility, ending medical intervention surgeries and other discriminatory practices perpetuated on intersex babies and persons.

dialogue-on-strengthening-child-protecti.title: Dialogue on strengthening child protection and addressing harmful practices affecting people with variations in sex development (Intersex people)
dialogue-on-strengthening-child-protecti.text:
Intersex Nigeria held an Intersectional Training Workshop aimed at strengthening the connections between Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), child rights, and intersex rights. This workshop brought together organizations across Nigeria that are actively working in these critical areas to explore intersectional approaches, share best practices, and build collaborations to eliminated Intersex Genital Mutilation (IGM), child abuse, and FGM.

The workshop featured key discussions with members of Child Protection Networks and FGM Networks, who aligned their efforts to protect intersex children from harmful medical and cultural practices. Participants examined existing laws and policies in Nigeria that address FGM, IGM, trafficking, and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV). Through these discussions, gaps were identified that leave intersex children particularly vulnerable to abuse, discrimination, and stigma.

The development of community-driven strategies aimed at integrating intersex issues into advocacy and programming was designed, and participants worked to formulate a joint action plan that outlines steps to advance inclusive policy reforms and grassroots interventions. They also committed to maintaining a partnership with Intersex Nigeria, ensuring that their efforts continue to evolve and adapt to the needs of intersex persons.

By bringing together diverse organizations, this workshop represents a significant step toward creating a safer, more inclusive environment for all children. Through ongoing efforts. Intersex Nigeria remains dedicated to fostering multi-sectoral partnerships that protect the rights and bodily autonomy of intersex children and all vulnerable groups in Nigeria.

national-youth-service-sensitization-you.title: National Youth Service Sensitization (Youth Focused Advocacy) 2025
national-youth-service-sensitization-you.text:
In April 2025, Intersex Nigeria continued its vital efforts to promote awareness, visibility, and sexual and reproductive health rights (SRHR) by visiting the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) orientation camp in Wannune, Tarka Local Government Area of Benue State, Nigeria. This continued initiative marked another significant stride in the organization's mission to foster understanding and inclusivity for intersex individuals.

During this visit, Intersex Nigeria held an impactful session in the NYSC hall through a seminar- style presentation that attracted over 1,700 corps members and carried out one-on-one sensitization sessions. The session constitutes learning, open conversations, and shared curiosity. Participants asked questions and engaged in discussions that highlighted the importance of recognizing intersex and the unique challenges faced by intersex individuals. There was an atmosphere of openness; the team dispelled myths and misconceptions surrounding intersex existence.

These visits are not just about raising awareness; it's about building a future where intersex inclusion is prioritized, and conversations about sexual and reproductive health rights are inclusive of all.

As Intersex Nigeria continues its journey, We are creating a future where intersex inclusion starts with awareness and education.

csos-stakeholders-engagement-in-makurdi-.title: CSOs Stakeholders' engagement in Makurdi, Benue State, Nigeria
csos-stakeholders-engagement-in-makurdi-.text:
In the move towards promoting intersex rights and inclusion, Intersex Nigeria engaged with 15 representatives from various Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) in Makurdi. This stakeholders' meeting laid the groundwork for Intersex Nigeria's ongoing efforts in Benue State.

During the sessions, Intersex Nigeria's team provides valuable knowledge on several key topics, and the team also focused on dispelling myths and misconceptions that often surround intersex individuals, which lead to discrimination and stigma.

A significant part of the discussion centered on understanding the different variations of intersex characteristics. This knowledge is essential for stakeholders who work directly with communities, as it enables them to approach intersex issues with sensitivity and understanding. The team also presented effective strategies for supporting intersex individuals, emphasizing the need for inclusion in community programs and initiatives. The team also highlighted existing gaps in laws, policies, and frameworks concerning intersex rights.

As Intersex Nigeria continues its advocacy work, the collaboration with CSOs in Benue State represents a promising step forward. By bringing together diverse organizations and fostering a shared understanding of intersex issues, Together, we are striving towards a society where every intersex individual is recognized and respected.

a-sensitization-workshop-for-the-federal.title: A Sensitization Workshop for the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare on Understanding Intersex and Inclusive Intersex Healthcare
a-sensitization-workshop-for-the-federal.text:
Intersex Nigeria hosted a workshop in Abuja with officials from the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, focusing on the need to include intersex individuals in healthcare planning and design. This engagement aimed to address barriers faced by intersex persons, such as unrecorded births, stigma in healthcare settings, and exclusion from essential healthcare services. 

The workshop brought together 34 representatives from various departments within the Ministry, creating discussions aimed at raising awareness and promoting inclusive healthcare policies. Participants explored strategic collaborations to enhance the well-being of intersex individuals and provide affirming healthcare services. 

A key objective was to bridge knowledge gaps and advocate for reforms that prioritize intersex rights. The officials called for the development of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to guide the protection and promotion of intersex health, along with specific healthcare policies or modifying existing ones that uphold their rights and dignity.

During the sessions, stakeholders emphasized the importance of evidence-based policy-making, urging collaboration with other institutions to address systemic issues in intersex healthcare. The need for a Social and Behavioral Change Communication (SBCC) plan was discussed, targeting media, policymakers, and the public to build understanding and acceptance of intersex issues.

Action points emerged from the workshop, including the integration of intersex perspectives into existing health policies. The workshop marked a significant step towards ensuring equitable healthcare access for intersex individuals in Nigeria.

national-youth-service-sensitization-you.title: National Youth Service Sensitization (Youth Focused Advocacy) 2024
national-youth-service-sensitization-you.text:
In May 2024, Intersex Nigeria continued its step forward in its mission to promote awareness and visibility by visiting the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) orientation camp in Kubwa, FCT Abuja. This initiative program aimed to educate young individuals about the understanding of sex characteristics and gender, as well as the lived realities of intersex persons in Nigeria.

Intersex Nigeria's team engaged several individuals in discussions that highlighted the need for visibility and understanding of intersex. By addressing prevalent myths and misconceptions surrounding intersex individuals in Nigeria.

During the visit, the team talked about the unique challenges and needs faced by intersex persons. They underscored the importance of preventing discrimination and promoting inclusion at all levels of society. This program not only aimed to educate the youth but also to cultivate empathy and support for intersex rights. A crucial topic of discussion was the alarming issue of Intersex Genital Mutilation (IGM). Intersex Nigeria is committed to advocating for the end of this harmful practice, which has long-term physical and psychological consequences.

The visit to the NYSC camp built a sense of empathy and solidarity among the reached youths and a community for intersex individuals.

media-engagement-on-positive-media-repre.title: Media Engagement on positive media representation of intersex persons in Nigeria.
media-engagement-on-positive-media-repre.text:
In April, Intersex Nigeria hosted a Media Engagement Workshop by bringing together journalists from leading media outlets in Nigeria. The primary focus of the workshop is to explore how the media can shift the narratives surrounding intersex individuals and enhance their visibility and rights in Nigeria.

The discussions were engaging, creating a collaborative environment where the journalists shared insights and experiences. Participants expressed a strong commitment to ensuring that intersex voices are heard and intersex issues are covered from an informed perspective, rather than through sensationalism. This change is crucial in creating an accurate portrayal of intersex individuals in media.

One of the outcomes of the event was to develop a comprehensive media toolkit. This toolkit is in creation with the journalists and will serve as a resource for guiding correct and informed reporting on intersex issues. By equipping journalists with the necessary tools and knowledge, we aim to create a media environment that respects intersex individuals.

This program is a step towards building better coverage and promoting inclusivity in media narratives. Through these efforts, we are paving the way for a future where intersex rights are recognized and celebrated.

national-youth-service-sensitization-you.title: National Youth Service Sensitization (Youth Focused Advocacy) 2023
national-youth-service-sensitization-you.text:
In August 2023, Intersex Nigeria started a dynamic sensitization program focused on youths in Nigeria, starting with the NYSC Camp in Lagos. This project was crafted to educate these young minds on the nuances of sex characteristics, gender identity, and the unique challenges faced by intersex persons. 

The sessions were informative and interactive, creating a lively atmosphere of curiosity and learning. Through a blend of enlightening presentations and engaging discussions, we discussed the misunderstood world of intersex persons, shedding light on their experiences and struggles. 

The program was an undeniable success. It wasn't just about imparting knowledge; it was about changing perceptions and creating a sense of responsibility among the young participants. We witnessed a remarkable transformation as attendees began to understand the importance of advocating for the rights of intersex persons. They left the sessions not only more informed but also more empathetic and committed to supporting the cause.

world-untold-echoes-of-silence---an-educ.title: “World Untold, Echoes Of Silence” - (An Educative And Entertaining Stage Play Project)
world-untold-echoes-of-silence---an-educ.text:
Intersex Nigeria presented 'World Untold: Echoes of Silence', a stage play in Abuja, Nigeria. This impactful stage play wove together personal stories, cultural reflections, and societal critiques, highlighting the diverse experiences of intersex persons. The play educated the audience about intersex issues, dispelling myths and promoting empathy. Authentic performances deeply moved the audience, creating a powerful emotional experience that resonated long after the curtain fell. 

The event united activists, allies, policymakers, and the intersex community,promoting a sense of solidarity and collective responsibility to advocate for intersex rights, as we recorded over four hundred guests physically from widespread across the country’s capital and its environs. 'World Untold: Echoes of Silence' created widespread of discussions, inspiring ongoing efforts for greater inclusion and equality. The play showcased the transformative power of art to educate, inspire, and drive social change, leaving an indelible mark on all who experienced its compelling narrative.

radio-sensitization-in-local-communities.title: Radio Sensitization in Local Communities
radio-sensitization-in-local-communities.text:
Intersex Nigeria embarked on an innovative radio outreach program, starting with Ikorodu FM, a widely popular station with a broad reach across Nigeria. This initiative was designed to leverage the power of radio to engage with diverse communities, including those in remote and underserved areas, to raise awareness about intersex issues. 

Our team carefully curated a series of engaging and informative segments aimed at educating the public about intersex variations, debunking myths and misconceptions, and highlighting the real-life experiences and challenges faced by intersex persons in Nigeria. A live call-in segment allowed listeners to ask questions and share their thoughts, promoting a sense of community and support. Indigenous Languages: The use of indigenous languages ensured that the message reached a wider audience, resonating deeply with local communities.

viral-project.title: VIRAL Project
viral-project.text:
The VIRAL Project stands for Visibility, Inclusion, and Recognition of Intersex Persons in Nigeria and Cameroon. This research aims to uncover the prevalence of intersex genital mutilation (IGM) and raise awareness of its consequences, extent, and scope in Nigeria and Cameroon. 

The 2nd of March 2023, marked the kick off of the VIRAL project, bringing together Human Rights Organizations, traditional rulers, religious leaders, state and non-state actors, law enforcement agents, the Human Rights Commission, and intersex persons in Nigeria. 

The meeting launched the VIRAL project and aiimed at raising awareness on the consequences, extent, and scope of intersex genital mutilation in Nigeria and Cameroon. Stakeholders committed to ensuring the successful implementation of the project.
